intro: A portable washer can end the laundromat run, but only if it hooks up to your faucet, drains where you need it to and fits your lease. Here are six worth buying and the plumbing details that decide which one works in your space.

A portable washer is not a small version of a full-size machine. It is a different tool with its own trade-offs: smaller loads, a temporary hookup to a sink, and a drain hose you have to think about every time. Get the hookup and the drain right and a good one will save you hours a week. Get them wrong and it becomes a heavy box in the closet.
quickAnswer: the BLACK+DECKER BPWM16W Portable Washer is our #1 pick (best overall portable washer). The default apartment pick: big enough to matter, small enough to store, and fully automatic once it is hooked up.

sections.h: What Actually Matters in a Portable Washer

blocks.p: Start with where the water comes from and where it goes. Every portable washer needs a supply, usually a kitchen or bathroom faucet through a quick-connect adapter, and a drain, usually the same sink, a tub or a standpipe. If your faucet cannot take an adapter, or your sink sits higher than the machine can pump, nothing else on the spec sheet matters. Look at your faucet and measure from the floor to the rim of the sink you plan to drain into before you shop.

Next is capacity, which manufacturers quote in cubic feet of drum volume and sometimes in pounds of dry laundry. Portable machines run from under 1 cu ft to around 2 cu ft. For scale, a typical full-size top-loader is well over 4 cu ft. A 1.6 cu ft machine handles a few days of clothes for one or two people; a 0.9 cu ft machine is closer to a single outfit plus towels. Buy for how often you are willing to run it, not for the biggest number you can fit.

Then decide how hands-on you want to be. A fully automatic portable fills, washes, rinses, spins and drains on its own once it is hooked up. A twin tub is cheaper and simpler but makes you fill it, move clothes from the wash tub to the spin tub and drain it yourself. Both clean clothes well. The difference is whether you can walk away from it, which matters more than most buyers expect.

Finally, think about the space itself. Portable washers sit on casters or feet and get rolled to the sink on laundry day, so you need a path, a level spot near the faucet and a floor that can take a little water. Upstairs apartments, older buildings and RVs add a layer of risk: a leak or a drain hose that pops out of the sink is your problem and possibly your neighbor's. A cheap drip pan and a habit of staying nearby solve most of that.

If you also need to dry clothes indoors, plan the pair together. A compact washer leaves clothes wetter than a full-size machine with a fast spin, which affects drying time on a rack or in a small dryer. Our [guide to portable dryers](/best-portable-dryer/) covers the 120V compact dryers that pair with these washers, and the venting rules that come with them.

sections.h: Twin Tub vs Fully Automatic: Which Type Fits

blocks.p: A twin tub washer has two compartments side by side. The larger one agitates clothes in water you add with a hose or bucket; the smaller one is a spin basket that wrings the water out after washing and again after rinsing. You set a timer on each side, move the clothes by hand between stages and drain the wash tub through a hose. It sounds primitive, and it is, but it is also cheap, light, quick and very forgiving about water supply.

The strengths of a twin tub are real. Because you control the water, you can fill it from any faucet with a hose, from a bucket, or from an RV tank, and you can reuse rinse water if you are conserving. The separate spinner is often the better part of the machine: owners commonly report that clothes come out of a twin tub spinner noticeably drier than out of a small automatic, which shortens drying time. Most twin tubs drain by gravity, which keeps them simple but limits where you can put the drain.

A fully automatic portable works like a scaled-down top-loader. You connect it to the faucet with a quick-connect adapter, put the drain hose in the sink, pick a cycle and leave. It handles fill, wash, rinse, spin and drain in sequence, usually with a few water levels and cycles for delicates, heavy items and quick washes. It costs more and weighs more, and it depends entirely on that faucet connection, but it gives you back your time.

For most apartment dwellers with a standard kitchen faucet, a fully automatic machine is the better buy. You start it, go do something else and come back to finished laundry. For RVers, campers, people without a compatible faucet and anyone on a tight budget, a twin tub makes more sense. It also suits people who wash small loads frequently, such as workout gear or baby clothes, because each run is short and you can stop at any point.
THE RULE
Buy automatic for convenience, twin tub for flexibility.

If your faucet takes a standard adapter and you want to walk away from the machine, buy fully automatic. If you need to fill from a bucket or tank, drain by gravity, or keep the cost and weight down, buy a twin tub and accept that you will be standing next to it.

The table below lines up the six picks on the specs that decide whether a machine works in your space. Capacities are the manufacturer figures where we are confident of them; where a listing varies or we could not confirm the number, we say to check it rather than guess. Pay most attention to the type and hookup columns, because those decide day-to-day use more than a few tenths of a cubic foot.

Two things the table cannot show are noise and balance. Small automatic washers spin a light drum on a light cabinet, and owners commonly report that they walk or bang during spin if the load is lopsided or the floor is uneven. Leveling the feet, splitting heavy items like jeans and towels across loads, and setting the machine on a firm surface instead of carpet all help. Twin tub spinners have the same issue and usually need you to arrange the clothes evenly in the basket.

Cycle count matters less than it looks. Most people use a normal cycle and a quick cycle and ignore the rest. What does matter is whether the machine offers more than one water level, so you are not filling the drum for a handful of items, and whether it has a dedicated spin-only setting for re-spinning clothes that came out too wet. Those two features save more water and drying time than a long list of named cycles.

If you are comparing against a combo washer-dryer, remember that an all-in-one is a different category: larger, heavier, usually permanently installed and priced well above any machine here. A portable washer plus a separate compact dryer or a drying rack is cheaper, more flexible and easier to move when you change apartments.

sections.h: Sink Faucet Adapters and Water Supply

blocks.p: Most fully automatic portables connect through a quick-connect faucet adapter. You unscrew the aerator from the tip of the faucet, screw on the adapter, and the washer's inlet hose snaps onto it. The adapter usually comes in the box with a couple of thread sizes, because faucet aerators come in male and female threads in a few common diameters. Unscrew your aerator before you buy and take it to a hardware store if you are not sure which you have.

Pull-out and pull-down sprayer faucets are the usual problem. Many have no removable aerator in a standard thread, or the sprayer head cannot hold a hose under pressure. Some owners solve this with an adapter matched to the sprayer, others run a short hose from a bathroom faucet or a utility sink, and some add a separate tee on the cold and hot supply lines under the sink. That last option is a plumbing change; in a rental, ask first, and if you are not comfortable working on supply lines, hire a plumber.

Temperature control is usually done at the faucet. A single inlet hose takes whatever mix you set at the tap, so for a warm wash you set the faucet warm before starting the fill. Some machines have separate hot and cold inlets, which works with a dual-hose setup but not with a single faucet adapter. Never leave the faucet turned on and walk away for long periods; when the wash is finished, turn off the tap and relieve the pressure before disconnecting the hose.

Water quality affects small machines more than you would think. Hard water leaves scale on the heating element if there is one and in the drum and pump, and sediment can clog the inlet screen. If you have hard or sandy water, cleaning the inlet screen every few weeks helps, and a whole-home or point-of-entry filter helps more. Our [guide to whole-house water filtration](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/) covers the options for apartments and houses, including what you can install without a permanent change.

Twin tubs and hand-crank washers skip most of this. You fill them with a hose from any faucet that will hold one, a kitchen sprayer held over the tub, or simply a bucket. That is why they are the default for RV and van owners and for anyone who cannot touch the plumbing. In an RV, keep an eye on your fresh-water tank level, because even a small wash and rinse can use more water than you expect.

sections.h: Drain Height, Drain Pumps and Gravity Drains

blocks.p: Draining is where portable washers trip people up. There are two ways water leaves the machine: a drain pump that pushes it up through the hose, or gravity, which only works when the end of the hose is lower than the outlet on the machine. Check the manual or listing for which one your model uses before you plan where it will sit, because it decides whether you can drain into a kitchen sink at all.

Pump-drain machines publish a maximum drain height, and you need to stay under it. A kitchen sink rim sits around three feet off the floor, and a bathtub rim much lower. If the drain hose has to climb higher than the pump is rated for, the machine drains slowly, leaves water in the drum or throws an error. Keep the hose free of kinks and avoid long horizontal runs, which add work for a small pump.

Gravity-drain machines, including most twin tubs, need the drain lower than the machine. That usually means a bathtub, a shower pan, a floor drain or a bucket. Some owners put the machine on a sturdy stand or in the tub itself so the hose can reach a sink. Do not stack it on anything that can tip during spin, and never let a gravity drain siphon into a sink that can overflow while you are out of the room.

Secure the hose end every time. A drain hose that is just hooked over a sink edge can jump out when the pump kicks on, and a full drum on the floor makes a mess fast. Clip it to the faucet, tie it to the sink with a strap or use a hose guide. Check that the sink drain itself is clear, because a slow drain will fill the basin faster than it empties. A lint catcher on the hose end protects the sink trap, and if it clogs anyway, our [drain snake guide](/best-drain-snake/) covers the hand tools that clear a sink trap without chemicals.

Lint is the long-term issue. Portable washers usually lack a large lint filter, so fibers go down the drain with the water. Over months that can slow the sink. A mesh lint trap on the end of the drain hose costs very little and catches most of it. Empty it after every load, and run hot water down the drain occasionally if you wash a lot of towels.

sections.h: Capacity in Cubic Feet: How Much Fits

blocks.p: Capacity numbers are useful but easy to misread. Cubic feet describes the drum volume; pounds describes the dry laundry the maker says the machine can wash. The two do not convert neatly, and brands round in their own favor. A practical rule is that a load should fill the drum loosely, with room for the clothes to move in the water. Pack it tight and the clothes come out wrinkled, unevenly washed and still soapy.

Around 0.9 cu ft is a single-person machine for frequent small loads: a few shirts, underwear and socks, or two bath towels. It suits a studio, a dorm or an RV where space is the constraint and you are willing to run it every day or two. Bulky items like comforters, heavy hoodies and full-size bath sheets will be a struggle or simply will not fit.

Around 1.6 cu ft is the sweet spot for most apartments. It handles a few days of clothes for one person or a couple, a set of sheets or a few towels at a time. This is the size most buyers should start with, because it is still light enough to roll to the sink and small enough to store in a closet, but it does not turn laundry into a daily chore.

Above about 2 cu ft, portable washers start to lose the portable part. They get heavier, harder to roll and harder to store, and you are closer to the price of a compact stackable washer that would need a real hookup. If you have a spot for a permanent machine and your lease allows it, a compact washer on proper supply and drain lines may be the better long-term choice.
Rough Load Guide
0.9 cu ft
Single person, daily small loads
1.6 cu ft
One or two people, a few days of clothes
2+ cu ft
Heavier, less portable
Loose
Clothes should move freely in the water

sections.h: Leases, Floors, and Running on a Generator or Power Station

blocks.p: Read your lease before you buy. Many leases prohibit washing machines outright or require written permission, mostly because of water damage risk. A portable machine that uses the sink is less risky than a permanent hookup, and many landlords will approve it if you ask. Get the approval in writing, and check that your renter's insurance covers water damage you cause, because a leak in an upstairs unit can damage the apartment below.

Protect the floor. Set the washer on a drip pan or a rubber mat, especially on wood, laminate or carpet. A washer pan with a lip will catch a small leak or a drain hose slip. Stay in the apartment while it runs; a small machine still uses several gallons per fill, and that is enough to soak a subfloor if the hose comes loose. When you are done, wipe out the drum and leave the lid open so it dries and does not grow mildew.

Electrically, a portable washer is a light load. It plugs into an ordinary 120V outlet and draws far less than a dryer or a space heater. Plug it into a grounded outlet, ideally a GFCI-protected one near the sink, as many kitchens and bathrooms already have. Avoid light-duty extension cords near water. If the outlet near your sink is not GFCI-protected, a licensed electrician can add protection, and in a rental that is the landlord's job.

Running a washer off grid is very doable. A modest portable power station can usually run a small washer, but motors pull a surge on start and spin, so check the watt rating on the washer's label and leave headroom on the station's continuous and surge ratings. A machine with a heater is a different story, because the heater draws much more. Our [portable power station guide](/best-portable-power-station/) covers sizing, and RVers will find the 12V side in our [power inverter guide](/best-power-inverter/).

A generator works too, but only outdoors. Never run a gas or propane generator indoors, in a garage, in an RV's living space or near open windows and doors, because carbon monoxide can kill. Run a heavy-duty outdoor-rated cord from the generator to the washer, and never plug a generator into a wall outlet to power the house. Inverter generators give cleaner power for electronic controls; our [RV generator guide](/best-rv-generator/) covers the quiet inverter models that suit campsites.

If you live in an apartment with a standard kitchen or bathroom faucet and want the machine to run itself, buy the BLACK+DECKER BPWM16W. It is the most widely available 1.6 cu ft fully automatic portable, it comes with the quick-connect faucet adapter, and it is big enough for one or two people without being a chore to move. The Magic Chef MCSTCW16W1 is the alternative at the same size if the BLACK+DECKER is out of stock or the price is better.

If space is the real limit, such as a studio closet, a dorm or a small RV with a shore-power hookup, buy the BLACK+DECKER BPWM09W. It does the same job in a smaller footprint, at the cost of smaller loads. If you want an automatic machine and value matters most, the Panda PAN56MGP3 is the budget automatic to compare, but confirm its capacity and drain method on the listing before you order.

If you do not have a compatible faucet, need to fill from a bucket or tank, or want the lowest price and the driest spin, buy the Giantex Twin Tub. It asks more of you at each step, but it is light, flexible and a good match for RVs and tiny houses. If you have no power at all, or wash delicates and small loads at camp, the Laundry Alternative Wonderwash does a surprising amount with a hand crank and a bucket of water.

Skip the very cheapest no-name automatic washers on marketplaces with thin listings and unclear model numbers. They are hard to get parts for, and if the pump or the control board fails, the machine is scrap. A known brand with a real model number and a manual you can download costs a little more and is far easier to keep running.

Whichever you buy, budget for a drip pan, a lint trap for the drain hose and, if your faucet is unusual, the right adapter. Those accessories cost very little and prevent most of the problems that make people give up on portable washers. If you need a matching dryer, our [portable dryer guide](/best-portable-dryer/) covers the 120V compact options and the venting they need.

mistakes: Pull-out sprayers and unusual aerators often will not take the included quick-connect adapter. Unscrew your aerator before you buy and confirm the thread type. If it does not fit, plan on a bathroom faucet, a utility sink or a properly installed supply tee, or buy a twin tub you can fill by hose or bucket.

A pump can only lift water so high, and a gravity drain cannot lift it at all. Measure the sink rim, check the manual's maximum drain height and the drain method, and choose the drain point before the machine arrives. A drain that cannot keep up leaves water in the drum and on the floor.

A hose hooked over the sink edge can jump out when the pump starts and dump a drum of water on the floor. Clip or strap it in place every time, add a lint trap and stay nearby while the machine drains, especially in an upstairs apartment where a leak becomes the neighbor's problem.

Cramming a 0.9 or 1.6 cu ft drum leaves soap in the clothes, unbalances the spin and strains the motor. Load loosely so items can move in the water, split heavy towels and jeans across loads, and use the spin-only setting if clothes still come out too wet.
Skipping the lease and insurance check

Many leases restrict washing machines, and water damage you cause is your liability. Ask your landlord in writing, confirm your renter's insurance covers accidental water damage and use a drip pan. A five-minute conversation now beats a long dispute over a stained ceiling in the unit downstairs later.
bottomLine: The best portable washer is the one that fits your faucet, drains where you need it to and matches how often you want to do laundry. For most apartments that is a 1.6 cu ft fully automatic machine like the BLACK+DECKER BPWM16W or the Magic Chef MCSTCW16W1, with the BPWM09W for tight spaces and the Panda PAN56MGP3 as the value automatic to compare. If you cannot use a faucet adapter, need to fill from a bucket or tank, or want the lowest price, the Giantex Twin Tub is the flexible choice, and the Wonderwash covers off-grid small loads. Whichever you pick, get permission in writing, put a pan under it, secure the drain hose and stay nearby while it runs.

faqs.q: What is the best portable washer for an apartment?
faqs.a: For most apartments with a standard faucet, a 1.6 cu ft fully automatic washer like the BLACK+DECKER BPWM16W or Magic Chef MCSTCW16W1 is the best fit. It is big enough for one or two people, runs itself once hooked to the sink and rolls into a closet afterwards. If you are short on space, the 0.9 cu ft BPWM09W does the same job with smaller loads.

faqs.q: Can I use a portable washer with any sink faucet?
faqs.a: Not always. Fully automatic portables connect with a quick-connect adapter that replaces the faucet aerator, and the included adapters fit common aerator threads. Pull-out and pull-down sprayer faucets often do not work. Check your aerator thread before buying. If it will not fit, use a bathroom or utility sink, add a supply tee with permission, or buy a twin tub you fill by hose.

faqs.q: Is a twin tub washer better than a fully automatic one?
faqs.a: It depends on how you live. A twin tub is cheaper, lighter, fills from any hose or bucket and usually spins clothes drier, but you move clothes between tubs and run each stage by hand. A fully automatic washer costs more and needs a compatible faucet, but you can start it and walk away. Most apartment dwellers prefer automatic; RVers often prefer twin tubs.

faqs.q: Is there a portable washer and dryer for an apartment?
faqs.a: Yes, though most people do better with a separate portable washer and a compact 120V dryer than with an all-in-one. All-in-one combos are larger, heavier and usually installed more permanently. A pair like a 1.6 cu ft portable washer and a compact dryer, or a washer plus a drying rack, is cheaper and easier to move. Check the dryer's venting requirements before you buy.

faqs.q: Can a portable washer run on a power station or generator?
faqs.a: Usually. A small washer without a heater is a light load, but its motor surges on start and spin, so check the watt rating on the label and leave headroom on the station's continuous and surge ratings. A generator works too, but only outdoors, well away from doors and windows, because of carbon monoxide. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet.

faqs.q: Do I need my landlord's permission for a portable washer?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many leases restrict or prohibit washing machines because of water damage risk, even portable ones. Read the lease, ask in writing and keep the reply. Landlords are often more comfortable with a sink-connected portable than a permanent hookup. Also check that your renter's insurance covers accidental water damage to your unit and the units around it.

faqs.q: How much water does a portable washer use?
faqs.a: It varies by model, water level and cycle, so check the manual for the specific machine. Small automatics use noticeably less water per load than full-size top-loaders, and twin tubs can use less still because you control the fill and can reuse rinse water. In an RV, watch your fresh-water tank level, because wash and rinse together can use more than you expect.
